community to abandon short-term, project-based climate financing in favor of predictable, multi-year funding to build permanent, nationally owned systems of resilience. speaking at the solutions dialogue on financing adaptation in the era of global overshoot at united nations headquarters in new york, atty. analiza rebuelta-teh, department of environment and natural resources (denr) undersecretary for finance, information systems, climate change and administration, highlighted the urgent need to sustain early warning capabilities so that alerts lead directly to protective action. for climate-vulnerable island nations like the philippines, “we are already confronting increasingly intense and compounding hazards that threaten lives, livelihoods, food and water security, ecosystems, and economic stability”, undersecretary rebuelta-teh said. the call comes as financial pressure mounts on developing countries. global adaptation costs for developing nations are projected to reach $310 billion to $365 billion annually by 2035—a burden amplified by widespread debt distress and high capital costs. in the philippines, delaying action carries a severe economic burden: inaction across eight priority sectors outlined in the national adaptation plan (nap) is estimated to cost the country ₱645 billion every year. “adaptation cannot remain reactive,” the undersecretary emphasized. “we need new, additional, predictable, and scaled-up public finance to enable developing countries to respond to growing climate risks at the speed and scale required.” to build sustainable financing for early warning infrastructure, rebuelta-teh outlined three priority areas: treating early warning systems as permanent public infrastructure: transitioning away from short-term project grants toward multi-year, predictable financing streams. funding last-mile action: securing pre-arranged, trigger-based funding alongside local risk data, warning distribution systems, and community preparedness programs to ensure alerts trigger immediate local protection. financing the “unfunded middle” and securing domestic ownership: providing resources for continuous operations, system maintenance, data collection, staff training, and technical upgrades, establishing a clear path toward full domestic budget integration. reinforcing its commitment to global disaster risk management, the philippines recently formalized its entry as the 71st member of the coalition for disaster resilient infrastructure (cdri), becoming only the second southeast asian nation to join the international organization. “for the philippines, our goal is to move from isolated projects to permanent, nationally owned systems of resilience,” undersecretary rebuelta-teh said. the archipelago strategy: how a philippine university network is blueprinting the future of higher education on a tropical midmorning in manila, where the relentless hum of traffic along the pasig river mirrors the rapid cadence of southeast asia's digital economy, a quiet structural revolution is reshaping how the developing world prepares its young for the future of work. across the philippine archipelago, some 75 million citizens comprise the working-age population, a demographic dividend that economists have long cited as the nation's greatest untapped growth engine. yet inside the lecture halls and executive suites of manila's top institutions, a stubborn paradox has persisted for decades: while higher education enrollments have expanded, the gap between academic curricula and the hyper-fluid demands of global industry has widened into a chasm. enter ipeople, inc. (pse:ipo), the educational holding vehicle under house of investments, inc. (pse:hi) and the prestigious yuchengco group of companies. rather than attempting to incrementally overhaul decades-old university syllabi through traditional, sluggish bureaucratic channels, ipeople took a radically pragmatic leap. through its flagship institutions, most notably mapúa university, long revered as the country's premier engineering and technological powerhouse, the group quietly integrated digital microcredentials, generative artificial intelligence skills, and industry certifications directly into its core degree programs. the bold gamble has paid off on a global stage. out of more than 780 higher education institutions evaluated across the globe, ipeople was named the sole recipient of coursera's global learning excellence award at the platform's marquee fwd event. the accolade recognizes visionary organizations that have fundamentally dismantled traditional barriers to higher education, proving that an emerging market network can out-innovate legacy institutions in western economies. “for the ipeople group of institutions, one of the things that we like to do is recognize exemplars,” says anthony salcito, senior vice president and president of enterprise at coursera, sitting down to reflect on the global milestone. “this is a very, very important time in the world of skilling as so many jobs are changing. reskilling has become an imperative across the 3.7 billion workers in jobs today, and the 75 million filipinos who are in the working-age labor force need to be reskilled and upskilled continually.” what began in 2019 as a pre-pandemic initiative to expand online course access has evolved into a sophisticated hybrid paradigm. today, the partnership reaches over 45,000 active learners annually across the ipeople system, with coursera's third-party coursework contributing to roughly 20 percent of students' required academic credits. in an era where artificial intelligence threatens to render traditional four-year degrees obsolete before the ink on a diploma can dry, ipeople's model offers a compelling blueprint for how higher education can survive and lead the age of automation. the speed of disruption vs. the slow grind of academia to understand why a university network in the philippines beat out hundreds of global rivals for top learning honors requires examining the acute structural crisis facing global higher education. historically, university faculty members have served as the ultimate guardians of knowledge. a professor drafts a syllabus, refines it over a decade, and delivers lecture material that remains relatively stable. but the exponential acceleration of software development, cloud computing, and now generative ai has dismantled that cadence. “one of the things that i think universities struggle with is creating a reason why, in many cases, getting faculty to understand how this is going to add value,” salcito explains with the seasoned authority of a veteran edtech executive. ai is increasingly tied to foundational soft skills, a relationship formalized in the company's recent job skills report under the “ai synergy index.” technical ai competencies, such as machine learning, prompt engineering, and agentic ai frameworks, are soaring in demand across regional industries. however, complementary human skills like critical thinking, complex problem-solving, and ethical reasoning are growing just as rapidly alongside them. while automated systems handle execution, industry leadership increasingly demands strategic oversight and holistic decision-making. for
